## 31. Workstream 4 — Decentralized Blockchain Access

### 31.1 Separate correctness from liveness, and the problem halves

The single most useful move in this workstream is a distinction the current
design already implies but never states:

```text
  CORRECTNESS  — "is this answer true?"       solved, by the light client
  LIVENESS     — "can I get an answer at all?" not solved, and it is the
                                                actual centralisation
```

`internal/ethproof` verifies sync-committee signatures and Merkle-Patricia
proofs, so a lying provider produces proofs that fail verification. **Correctness
is already trust-minimised and this workstream must not re-litigate it.** What
remains is that the PoF architecture routes every node's chain access through a
website-run External Node, paymaster and relayer, and the resolver needs a beacon
source and an RPC. Those are single points of *observation, censorship and
unavailability*, and none of them can be fixed by a better proof.

| Property | Status | Attack that remains |
|---|---|---|
| Provider cannot lie about state | **Solved** — `VerifyProof` against a light-client-verified `stateRoot` | None; a lie is a detectable failure |
| Provider cannot lie about absence | **Solved** — absence proofs terminate at the first divergent node (160 B, measured) | None |
| Provider cannot refuse | **Not solved** | Selective refusal, targeted at one node or one name |
| Provider cannot stall | **Not solved** | Freshness attack: serve only old-but-valid state |
| Provider cannot observe | **Not solved** | The relayer sees every registration; the RPC sees every query |
| Provider cannot be the only one | **Not solved** | Single External Node in the PoF design |
| Broadcast is verifiable | **Not solvable** — noted in `doc/ethereum-data-layer.md` §7 | A provider can accept a transaction and not broadcast it; only later inclusion is verifiable |

### 31.2 The mechanism: three sources, and chain evidence carried by AXON itself

**(a) `k_src` independent sources for liveness.** Correctness needs one source;
liveness needs several. Independence is defined structurally, not by count:
distinct operator, distinct ASN, and — where possible — distinct client
implementation. `k_src = 3` is the floor, and the existing
`SetAnchor → ErrAnchorNotIndependent` rule (which refuses an anchor sharing a
registrable domain with the RPC) is exactly the right shape and should be
generalised to the source set.

**(b) Chain evidence distributed over AXON's own DHT.** This is the structural
fix, and the arithmetic is already measured in `doc/ethereum-data-layer.md`:

```text
  sync-committee updates    ~7.6 MB / year     append-only, immutable
  verified headers          ~2.7 GB / year     append-only, immutable
  storage proofs            on demand          immutable, cacheable
```

All of it is content-addressed and never rewritten — precisely what the storage
layer is for, and the P12-3 plan already anticipated putting it there. A node
that has the header chain and the committee updates **needs no RPC to verify a
read it has a proof for**, and proofs themselves are cacheable objects. The
dependency collapses from "an RPC provider" to "any source of immutable
append-only data", which the overlay is.

**(c) The relayer made optional and non-observing.** The PoF meta-transaction
design (`registerWithSig`, owner recovered on-chain) is already correct in that
the relayer cannot name the owner. What it lacks is plurality and privacy:
several independent relayers discovered through the DHT, self-submission always
available as a fallback, and submission over a circuit so the relayer learns a
transaction but not its origin.

### 31.3 The seventeen fields

| Field | Content |
|---|---|
| **Threat model** | The RPC or relayer operator; an adversary who can block access to them; a network position that isolates a node from the chain; and Ethereum itself as a systemic dependency |
| **Current AXON weakness** | Liveness, observation and censorship all rest on single providers; the PoF architecture explicitly centralises node chain access in a website-run stack |
| **Security objective** | (a) No single source causes an incorrect answer — already met, re-verified. (b) No single source causes unavailability: `k_src ≥ 3` independent. (c) `S_max` declared per resolver mode and enforced. (d) Recovery from prolonged isolation is specified and tested |
| **Candidate mechanisms** | Multi-source proof-carrying reads; chain evidence in the DHT; DHT-discovered execution endpoints; rotating providers; quorum on *availability* rather than on truth; local cached verified state; checkpoint diversity from mutually independent origins; relayer plurality with self-submission fallback |
| **Mechanisms rejected** | **Quorum voting on state values** — `doc/trust-anchor.md` §5C already rules that N-of-M provider agreement "must not be described as verification", and it is right: agreement among providers is not evidence, and adopting it would weaken a property the system already has. **A single canonical AXON RPC** — the centralisation being removed. **Running a full execution node per AXON node** — `doc/p146-local-execution-node.md` measured this and concluded it does not fit the infrastructure |
| **Protocol changes** | A `ChainEvidence` record class in the DHT (headers, committee updates, proofs); endpoint discovery records; a source-independence policy object |
| **Cryptographic changes** | None. BLS, SSZ and MPT verification exist and are mainnet-exercised |
| **DHT changes** | Bulk append-only evidence storage — ~2.7 GB/year is a real load and its retention policy, sharding and pruning must be specified against the erasure-coding parameters |
| **Economic changes** | Evidence storage and relaying are services the accounting plane can pay for, which is a natural fit for §14 but must not become a requirement for correctness |
| **Implementation changes** | `blockchain/sources.go` (multi-source with independence policy), `blockchain/evidence.go` (DHT publication and retrieval), `blockchain/relayers.go`, and generalising `ErrAnchorNotIndependent` to the whole source set |
| **Simulation methodology** | Fault injection over source availability: single-source failure, correlated failure by ASN, targeted refusal for one name, freshness attack, and total isolation for 1 h / 1 d / 1 w |
| **Adversarial test methodology** | A hostile provider container that serves valid-but-stale state, that refuses selectively for one `nameHash`, and that colludes with a second source; plus a partition that isolates chain access while leaving the overlay intact — the combined P3/P4 case |
| **Metrics** | `k_src` achieved in practice; `S_max` distribution under fault; probability of undetected staleness; time to recovery after isolation; fraction of reads servable from DHT evidence with no RPC |
| **Milestones** | M4.1 source-independence policy and multi-source client. M4.2 chain evidence published to and retrieved from the DHT. M4.3 relayer plurality and self-submission. M4.4 freshness-attack detection. M4.5 isolation-recovery test. M4.6 the §31.5 dependency statement |
| **Exit criteria** | E4.1 A read completes correctly with any `k_src − 1` sources hostile or absent — falsified by a single-source dependency found in the code path. E4.2 A stale-but-valid source is detected within `S_max` and reported, not silently used. E4.3 A node with no RPC access at all completes a verified read from DHT-carried evidence. E4.4 Registration completes without the website relayer. E4.5 After one week of total chain isolation, a node recovers to a verified head, and the resolver's behaviour during isolation matches §13.6 exactly |
| **Residual risks** | Broadcast remains unverifiable. The weak-subjectivity checkpoint remains a subjective input, and checkpoint diversity reduces but does not remove it. Evidence in the DHT is only as available as the DHT, which couples P4 to P3 in both directions. Ethereum itself — §31.5 |
| **New attacks introduced** | **Evidence-store poisoning** — invalid headers offered as DHT objects, cheap to serve and cheap to reject, so it is a bandwidth-waste attack rather than a correctness one. **Endpoint-discovery manipulation** — an adversary that controls DHT records for endpoints steers a node to its own sources, which is the P3 attack wearing a P4 costume and is why the two share a phase. **Independence-policy gaming** — sources that appear independent by ASN and are not |

### 31.4 What this workstream does NOT establish

- That broadcast can be verified. It cannot, and the asymmetry belongs in the
  challenge budget, as `doc/ethereum-data-layer.md` already says.
- That the initial checkpoint can be made objective. Weak subjectivity is
  inherent.
- That DHT-carried evidence is cheaper than an RPC. It is more *independent*;
  at ~2.7 GB/year it is certainly not lighter, and the trade must be stated.
- That the PoF relayer's privacy leak is closed. Submitting over a circuit hides
  the origin from the relayer, not the fact of the registration from the chain.

### 31.5 Is Ethereum a hidden central dependency? Yes, and here is the bound

The honest answer, which the roadmap must not soften: **while namespace ownership
is settled on Ethereum, an Ethereum-level failure is an AXON namespace failure.**
No amount of light-client verification changes that; it makes the dependency
*honest*, not absent.

What is bounded, and how:

| Ethereum event | AXON consequence | Bound |
|---|---|---|
| Provider censors one node | None | `k_src ≥ 3` |
| All reachable providers refuse | Resolution degrades to SNAPSHOT mode | Bounded by `S_max`; names keep resolving, registrations stop |
| Chain halts / does not finalise | No ownership changes; existing bindings hold | Indefinite for reads; registration and transfer unavailable |
| Deep reorg past finality | A recently transferred name may flip | §13.6's reorg window; reads at finalised head only |
| Contentious fork | Two namespaces exist | Unresolvable technically; resolvers pin a chain, and this is the §12.0a fork right in a new costume |
| Gas price spike | Registration becomes unaffordable | A censorship outcome by price; noted in §23 P9 |
| Ethereum ceases | Ownership becomes unupdatable, and the last snapshot is the permanent record | Services remain reachable at Layer 1 (§11.9) — which is the entire reason Layer 1 is the guarantee |

The last row is the design's answer to its own worst case, and it is why §11's
three-layer model is load-bearing rather than decorative.

## 32. Workstream 5 — Traffic-Analysis Resistance

### 32.1 Two problems that must never be reported as one

| | Website fingerprinting (WF) | Flow correlation |
|---|---|---|
| Adversary position | **One** point — the client's link or its guard | **Both** ends |
| Question asked | "Which of a known set of destinations is this?" | "Are these two flows the same flow?" |
| Realistic defence | Padding and shaping measurably degrade it | Padding barely moves it |
| Expected AXON outcome | **BOUNDED** at stated overhead | **IMPOSSIBLE** at acceptable latency |

Reporting a padding scheme's benefit against WF as though it were a benefit
against correlation is the standard overclaim in this field, and §27.2's
pre-registration rule exists partly to prevent it here.

### 32.2 The base-rate discipline

WF results reported as closed-world accuracy are close to meaningless for a
deployed system. In an open world the quantity that matters is **precision at the
realistic prior**:

```text
  precision = TPR·p / ( TPR·p + FPR·(1−p) )

  p = 10⁻³ , TPR = 0.99 , FPR = 0.01  →  precision ≈ 0.090
  p = 10⁻³ , TPR = 0.95 , FPR = 0.001 →  precision ≈ 0.487
  p = 10⁻⁵ , TPR = 0.99 , FPR = 0.01  →  precision ≈ 0.001
```

A classifier with 99 % accuracy can be useless or decisive depending entirely on
the prior. **Every WF result this programme reports must state `p`, TPR, FPR and
precision.** Accuracy alone is not an acceptable report and a milestone that
produces only accuracy has not been met.

### 32.3 The AXON-specific finding: BULK traffic is free cover for INTERACTIVE

Cover traffic's problem everywhere it has been proposed is that it is pure waste:
bandwidth spent to carry nothing. **AXON is unusual in carrying two traffic
classes in one network, and one of them is bulk, continuous, latency-tolerant,
and doing real work** — erasure-coded shard transfer, repair, rebalancing, and
chain-evidence distribution (§31.2b), which is by itself ~2.7 GB/year per
participating node.

That suggests a mechanism that does not exist in Tor, I2P or Freenet because none
of them has both halves in the same network:

```text
   Conventional cover traffic:     pay bandwidth  →  get cover        (waste)
   AXON proposal:                  do storage work →  get cover free  (dual use)

   INTERACTIVE cells are multiplexed into circuits already carrying BULK
   shard traffic, at a shaped aggregate rate. The BULK flow is the padding,
   and it is padding that is simultaneously transferring real shards.
```

Properties to establish, and none of them is assumed:

1. **Does it actually help?** The BULK flow must be shaped so that adding
   interactive cells does not change the observable envelope. If it does, the
   cover is illusory and the mechanism is refuted.
2. **What does it cost the interactive stream?** Multiplexing into a shaped bulk
   flow adds latency and jitter. If it pushes interactive latency past usability
   the mechanism is refuted for that class.
3. **Does it leak the class anyway?** A relay carrying the merged flow may still
   distinguish. This is the primary experiment.
4. **Is it available?** A node doing no storage work has no cover. The mechanism
   is only as good as the node's participation, which makes it *incentive-linked*
   in a way the accounting plane can act on.

This is marked `[NEEDS RESEARCH]` and it is the most promising original idea in
the programme. It could also fail entirely on point 1.

### 32.4 The seventeen fields

| Field | Content |
|---|---|
| **Threat model** | Observes packet timing, size, direction, volume, duration, burst structure, circuit creation, and endpoint availability. WF adversary at one point; correlation adversary at both. Classifier-equipped, including modern deep-learning classifiers |
| **Current AXON weakness** | Fixed cells remove per-message length only. No padding machine, no shaping, no defended traffic class. R2 declares `INTERACTIVE` undefended and §16 defers everything meaningful |
| **Security objective** | **WF:** classifier precision below a pre-registered threshold at `p = 10⁻³`, at ≤ 50 % bandwidth overhead and ≤ 100 ms added median latency. **Correlation:** produce the measured curve and, if the expected result holds, state the impossibility explicitly rather than shipping a defence that does not work |
| **Candidate mechanisms** | Circuit-level padding machines with negotiated state machines; constant-rate shaping for `BULK`; adaptive/congestion-aware padding; the §32.3 dual-use cover; burst suppression; circuit scheduling; dummy circuits; delayed publication for the storage layer; traffic splitting across disjoint paths |
| **Mechanisms rejected** | **Constant-rate for `INTERACTIVE`** — the overhead and latency are incompatible with R2's class definition; it works, and it is not deployable. **"Add padding" without a state machine** — unmeasurable and historically ineffective. **Per-packet mixing for `INTERACTIVE`** — this is a mixnet, and R2 already ruled |
| **Protocol changes** | Padding-machine negotiation in the circuit handshake; a padding cell command already reserved in §8.1; class-aware scheduling at the relay |
| **Cryptographic changes** | None. Padding cells are indistinguishable from data cells by construction under §8.3's per-hop AEAD, which is a property worth stating explicitly here |
| **DHT changes** | None |
| **Economic changes** | Padding consumes relay bandwidth that the accounting plane would otherwise pay for; if §14 exists, padding must be compensated or relays will disable it. This is a real incentive conflict and it belongs in §33's calibration |
| **Implementation changes** | `tunnels/padding.go` (machines), `tunnels/schedule.go` (class-aware), plus a capture harness producing labelled traces |
| **Simulation methodology** | Packet-level simulation at small scale (10²–10³ nodes) — explicitly a *different* simulator from the Monte-Carlo path-selection model of §28, and §36 keeps them separate rather than pretending one tool does both |
| **Adversarial test methodology** | Evaluate against both statistical attacks and current deep-learning classifiers, in closed and open world, with the classifier **trained on defended traces** — evaluating a defence against a classifier trained on undefended traffic is the standard way to produce a fake result |
| **Metrics** | TPR, FPR, precision at stated `p`; mutual information between trace and destination; bandwidth overhead; added median and p99 latency; correlation TPR at fixed FPR for the two-ended adversary |
| **Milestones** | M5.1 trace capture harness and a labelled dataset from the local network. M5.2 baseline attack results on undefended AXON traffic. M5.3 padding machines implemented. M5.4 defended-trace evaluation with retrained classifiers. M5.5 §32.3 dual-use cover experiment. M5.6 correlation study and the explicit statement of its result |
| **Exit criteria** | E5.1 A baseline exists: attack performance against undefended AXON traffic, reported with precision at stated `p`. E5.2 A defence configuration meets the pre-registered WF threshold within the overhead budget — **falsified by the sweep, and failure here is an expected and acceptable outcome**. E5.3 The correlation result is published whatever it shows. E5.4 The §32.3 experiment returns a yes or a no, and a no is written into §40.4. E5.5 No defence is recommended on closed-world accuracy |
| **Residual risks** | End-to-end correlation. Endpoint availability patterns, which no padding hides. Application-layer behaviour above L8, entirely outside AXON's control |
| **New attacks introduced** | **Padding-machine fingerprinting** — the negotiated machine is itself a distinguisher, and a rare configuration identifies its user; machines must be few and defaults strong. **Class distinguishability** — `BULK` and `INTERACTIVE` are visibly different at a relay unless §32.3 works, so the traffic-class API of §20 may itself be a leak. **Padding as a DoS vector** — a client that negotiates expensive padding on many circuits consumes relay capacity for free |

### 32.5 What this workstream does NOT establish

- Protection against an adversary observing both ends. The expected deliverable
  is a measurement and a statement, not a defence.
- Protection above L8. Application behaviour is the dominant real-world leak and
  §18.21 already says so.
- That defended-trace results generalise. A classifier published after this work
  may defeat the defence, and WF results have a poor track record of aging well.
- Anything about the deployed network. Traces from a 100-node lab have no
  established relationship to a real population.

### 32.6 Comparison

| Source | Classification | What changes in AXON | Property that does not transfer |
|---|---|---|---|
| Tor — circuit padding framework / WTF-PAD lineage | `MODIFIED` | Adopted as the negotiation and machine model | Its calibration, which was done against Tor's traffic mix, not one containing continuous bulk storage traffic |
| Mixnets (Nym and the Loopix lineage) — Poisson mixing, loop cover | `REJECTED` for `INTERACTIVE`, `CANDIDATE` for `BULK` | Latency budget; R2's class split makes partial adoption coherent | Mixnet-grade unlinkability. Adopting the mechanism for `BULK` does not license the claim for anything else |
| Constant-rate defences (the BuFLO/Tamaraw lineage) | `REJECTED` as default, retained as the upper bound in the overhead study | They work; the cost is the problem | — |
| Freenet — bulk, latency-tolerant traffic | `NEW` in combination | §32.3's dual-use cover is only possible because AXON carries both classes | Freenet does not have a low-latency class to protect, so the idea has no analogue there |

## 33. Workstream 6 — Economic and Sybil Calibration

### 33.1 The finding: the weighting function decides everything, and it is a trilemma

Let an entity hold total stake `S` and split it across `k` identities. Under a
weighting function `w(·)` applied per identity, its total selection weight is
`k · w(S/k)`. The behaviour of that expression is not a detail:

| `w(s)` | `k·w(S/k)` vs `w(S)` | Effect on splitting | Effect on concentration |
|---|---|---|---|
| Concave, e.g. `√s` | `√(kS) > √S` — **increases with k** | **Rewards Sybils** | Resists plutocracy |
| Linear, `s` | `S` — **invariant** | Neutral | Neutral: weight ∝ capital |
| Convex, e.g. `s²` | `S²/k < S²` — **decreases with k** | Penalises Sybils | **Amplifies plutocracy** |

**The result, stated plainly: stake weighting alone cannot be simultaneously
Sybil-resistant and anti-plutocratic.** Concave weighting — the obvious choice
for limiting whale dominance, and the one quadratic-voting intuitions suggest —
actively pays an adversary to fragment into many identities, which is the exact
behaviour Sybil resistance is meant to prevent. This is a modelling result, not a
formal theorem, and it holds for any per-identity weighting; it is the reason
§15's "bonded stake" needs calibration before it can be called a defence.

**The escape is a per-identity fixed cost.** With a minimum bond `B_min`, an
entity can create at most `k ≤ S/B_min` identities, so concave weighting's
splitting reward is capped:

```text
   max weight  =  (S/B_min) · w(B_min)      for concave w
   choose B_min such that this is acceptable, and the design becomes:

       concave weighting          (limits whale dominance)
     + minimum bond floor B_min   (caps the splitting reward)
     + diversity constraints      (caps identities per /24 and per ASN)
     + lock period L > epoch      (defeats borrowed capital)
```

That combination is defensible. Each term without the others is not.

### 33.2 The cost formula

For selection weight linear in effective stake, with honest stake `S_h`, an
adversary seeking fraction `x` of selection probability must hold

```text
   S_a  =  x·S_h / (1 − x)

   x = 0.01 →  0.0101·S_h        x = 0.20 →  0.250·S_h
   x = 0.05 →  0.0526·S_h        x = 0.30 →  0.429·S_h
   x = 0.10 →  0.111·S_h
```

and the cost of holding it for `y` epochs with lock period `L`:

```text
   C(x,y)  =  S_a · r · (y+L)/E     opportunity cost at rate r, E epochs/year
            +  P_slash · S_a         expected slashing
            +  N_prefix · c_infra    diversity-constrained infrastructure
   where N_prefix ≥ (identities required) and c_infra is per-prefix/per-ASN cost
```

Two consequences the workstream must confront rather than report neutrally:

- **`C` is dominated by `S_h`.** Security is proportional to how much honest
  capital is locked, which is a quantity the protocol does not control and cannot
  predict. A network with little staked value is cheap to attack regardless of
  the mechanism's elegance.
- **`C` is an opportunity cost, not an expenditure.** An adversary who does not
  get slashed keeps the principal. The real price of a one-year 20 % attack is
  `0.25·S_h·r` — at `r = 5 %`, roughly **1.25 % of the honest stake**, recoverable
  in full. That is much cheaper than "you must acquire 25 % of the stake" makes
  it sound, and stating it this way is the workstream's most important output.

### 33.3 The seventeen fields

| Field | Content |
|---|---|
| **Threat model** | Large capital; many small identities; borrowed or flash capital; cartels of independent operators; compromised legitimate nodes; and an adversary optimising jointly across §33 and §35 (buy some capacity, fake the rest) |
| **Current AXON weakness** | §15's layered defence is uncalibrated and directionally unexamined; no `B_min`, no `L`, no weighting function, no `C(x,y)`. The interaction in §33.1 has never been checked |
| **Security objective** | `C(x = 0.20, y = 30 epochs)` computed and defended, with the derivation and the sensitivity to `S_h` published |
| **Candidate mechanisms** | Concave weighting + `B_min` + diversity caps + lock period `L`; capacity-bounded claims (§35); slashing on detected misbehaviour; identity age as a weight; randomised selection so an adversary cannot choose its position (§8.7) |
| **Mechanisms rejected** | **Pure proof-of-work admission** — pays a permanent energy cost for a one-time barrier and is trivially rented. **Unbounded delegation** — concentrates weight while distributing the appearance of it; if adopted at all it must be capped, and the cap is the mechanism. **Reputation without stake** — bootstraps from nothing, so a patient adversary simply waits |
| **Protocol changes** | Weighting function published as a network parameter (chain-anchored, per §22's upgrade mechanism); descriptor carries bond reference and lock expiry |
| **Cryptographic changes** | None |
| **DHT changes** | Bond references must be checkable without a chain call on the hot path — §7.9 already requires this and this workstream makes it load-bearing |
| **Economic changes** | This *is* the economic change: `B_min`, `L`, `w(·)`, slashing conditions, diversity caps, all calibrated jointly and all reusing `StakeVault` |
| **Implementation changes** | `accounting/weight.go`; selection integration in `routing/select.go`; bond verification cache |
| **Simulation methodology** | Adversary-optimisation model: given a budget, solve for the allocation across stake, identities, prefixes and faked capacity that maximises `x`. **The simulation must optimise on the adversary's behalf**, because evaluating a fixed naive strategy produces a flattering and useless number |
| **Adversarial test methodology** | Flash-capital attack across an epoch boundary; cartel formation; delegation concentration; joint optimisation with §35's measurement attack |
| **Metrics** | `C(x,y)` surface; sensitivity `∂C/∂S_h`; maximum `x` achievable at fixed budget; splitting gain under the chosen `w` |
| **Milestones** | M6.1 the §33.1 analysis reviewed and either confirmed or corrected. M6.2 parameter search over `(w, B_min, L, caps)`. M6.3 adversary optimiser. M6.4 `C(x,y)` published with sensitivity. M6.5 parameters proposed with the plutocracy statement attached |
| **Exit criteria** | E6.1 `C(0.20, 30)` is published as a formula in `S_h`, `r` and `c_infra`, with worked values at three plausible `S_h`. E6.2 The chosen `w` and `B_min` demonstrably cap splitting gain below a pre-registered factor. E6.3 A flash-capital adversary cannot acquire epoch weight — falsified by any successful cross-epoch attack. E6.4 The adversary optimiser finds no allocation beating the analytic bound by more than a pre-registered margin. E6.5 **The write-up states, in plain language, the degree to which the mechanism is pay-to-control** |
| **Residual risks** | Plutocracy is not eliminated, only priced. Security scales with honest stake, which the protocol cannot control. A wealthy adversary with no need to profit is unaffected by opportunity cost |
| **New attacks introduced** | **Bond-driven centralisation of high-value roles** — §28's layered guards require higher bonds, so the most security-critical positions are held by the wealthiest operators. **Slashing as an attack** — if slashing conditions are gameable, an adversary destroys honest operators' bonds. **Lock-period rigidity** — a long `L` deters honest participation more reliably than it deters a funded adversary |

### 33.4 What this workstream does NOT establish

- That AXON is Sybil-resistant. It establishes a price, and §40.4 records that a
  price is not the same thing.
- That the price is high enough. That depends on `S_h`, which is unknown and,
  for a new network, small.
- Anything about non-economic Sybil defence. The prefix and diversity terms of
  §15 are bounded by cloud-address economics, which this workstream measures but
  does not improve.
- That the concavity result is a theorem. It is a modelling argument and should
  be reviewed as one.

## 34. Workstream 7 — Anonymity-Set Size and Effective Anonymity

### 34.1 The finding: guards cut the anonymity set by two to three orders of magnitude

The specification has never stated an anonymity set, and the number is worse than
the reader would assume. Consider an adversary observing traffic at a guard it
controls. The candidate users are not "everyone on the network" — they are the
users who selected that guard. With `U` users each pinning `g` guards drawn from
`R` relays:

```text
   expected users behind one guard  ≈  U · g / R
```

| `U` | `R` | `g` | Users per guard = `A_eff` at the guard | Naive "network size" claim |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 10⁵ | 1 000 | 2 | **200** | 100 000 |
| 10⁵ | 5 000 | 2 | **40** | 100 000 |
| 10⁴ | 1 000 | 2 | **20** | 10 000 |
| 10³ | 200 | 2 | **10** | 1 000 |

**A user is anonymous among hundreds, not among the network.** And under
bandwidth-weighted selection the distribution is far from uniform: users
concentrate on high-capacity relays, so a user who happens to pin a *low*-capacity
guard is in a set of single digits. The worst case, not the average, is what a
targeted user experiences, which is why this workstream reports min-entropy
alongside entropy.

Note what this does to §28. Guards reduce `P_dea` — the probability of *ever*
touching a hostile relay — and simultaneously reduce `A_eff` — the number of
people you look like once one is touched. **They are the same mechanism producing
opposite effects on the two metrics, and no configuration optimises both.** §28.3
and this section are therefore required to report each other's number, and §37
records the joint frontier rather than two independent targets.

### 34.2 The definitions

Anonymity is a property of the adversary's posterior distribution over
candidates, not a count of participants (the Serjantov–Danezis formulation, and
the Díaz *et al.* line of work on entropy-based anonymity metrics):

```text
   after observation O, adversary holds  p(i | O)  over candidate set  C

   H    = − Σ p(i|O) log₂ p(i|O)            average-case uncertainty
   H∞   = − log₂ max_i p(i|O)               worst-case: the most likely suspect
   A_eff = 2^H          (average)      A_eff∞ = 2^H∞      (worst case)
   d    = 1 − H / log₂|C|                   degree of anonymity lost
```

`H∞` is the number a targeted user should be told. A system with `H = 8` bits
(`A_eff = 256`) and `H∞ = 2` bits (`A_eff∞ = 4`) is not a system in which anyone
is anonymous among 256 people; it is one in which the adversary's top suspect
carries probability 0.25.

### 34.3 Anonymity is measured per role, and the roles differ enormously

| Role | Candidate set | What shrinks it | Expected `A_eff` |
|---|---|---|---|
| **User (sender)** | Users sharing the observed guard | Guard pinning, timing, traffic class, isolation context | Hundreds at best (§34.1) |
| **Service (recipient)** | Services reachable at the observation time | Availability pattern, descriptor timing, intro-point set, popularity | Small; a rare service is nearly unique |
| **Relay operator** | Relays with similar capacity and position | Descriptor contents are public by design | Effectively 1 — relays are not anonymous and never claimed to be |
| **Storage provider** | Holders of a shard | Placement diversity constraints deliberately spread holders | Bounded by `r = 8` |
| **Request** | Requests in the same batch or window | Batching for `BULK`; nothing for `INTERACTIVE` | 1 for interactive |
| **Domain** | Names in the namespace | **Registration is public on chain** | Effectively 1 — §18 already says the domain list is public |
| **Session** | Sessions sharing a circuit | Per-destination isolation deliberately separates them | Small by design |
| **Circuit** | Circuits at a relay in the same interval | Multiplexing, padding | Depends entirely on §32 |

Three of these are effectively 1 and always were. **The document's job is to say
so** rather than let a reader assume a uniform anonymity property across roles —
`d` for a relay operator is 0, and that is a design choice, not a failure.

### 34.4 The seventeen fields

| Field | Content |
|---|---|
| **Threat model** | Parameterised by adversary class from §4; the metric is always stated relative to a specific observation by a specific class, since an unconditioned anonymity number is meaningless |
| **Current AXON weakness** | No model, no metric, no measurement. Every anonymity statement elsewhere in the specification is therefore qualitative, including several that read as though they were quantitative |
| **Security objective** | A measurement capability, not a threshold: `H`, `H∞`, `A_eff` computed per role per adversary class, on demand, from a network configuration. Thresholds are set per deployment once the instrument exists |
| **Candidate mechanisms** (for raising it) | Guard sharing — fewer, larger guard sets shared by more users; popularity equalisation for services; batching and delayed forwarding for `BULK`; service replication behind one `ServiceIdentity`; multi-intro-point services; circuit reuse within an isolation context; the §32.3 dual-use cover |
| **Mechanisms rejected** | **Counting nodes** — the error this workstream exists to correct. **Reporting `H` without `H∞`** — hides the targeted case. **Uniform-prior models** — bandwidth weighting makes the prior sharply non-uniform, and assuming uniformity flatters every result |
| **Protocol changes** | None required for measurement. Guard-sharing and popularity-equalisation mechanisms would change selection policy if adopted |
| **Cryptographic changes** | None |
| **DHT changes** | None for measurement. Descriptor-fetch timing is an input to the service-side model and may motivate fetch padding |
| **Economic changes** | None directly. §33's weighting determines the selection prior, hence the anonymity distribution, so the two must be evaluated together |
| **Implementation changes** | An offline analysis tool consuming a network configuration and an adversary specification, emitting the metric set. **Not** a runtime component: computing live anonymity metrics on a node would require exactly the global view the design refuses, and would itself be a leak |
| **Simulation methodology** | Analytic where tractable (guard-sharing distributions), Monte-Carlo otherwise; realistic bandwidth distributions drawn from measured relay populations where available, and flagged as synthetic where not |
| **Adversarial test methodology** | Compute the posterior an adversary can actually form given each observation type, rather than assuming it is uniform over the candidate set — including the compound observation of guard position plus timing plus traffic class |
| **Metrics** | `H`, `H∞`, `A_eff`, `A_eff∞`, `d`, per role, per adversary class, per network size |
| **Milestones** | M7.1 formal model and definitions, reviewed. M7.2 the tool. M7.3 baseline measurement of the current design at `U ∈ {10³, 10⁴, 10⁵}`. M7.4 guard-topology frontier jointly with §28. M7.5 mechanism evaluation. M7.6 publication of the per-role table with real numbers |
| **Exit criteria** | E7.1 The tool produces `H` and `H∞` for all eight roles at three network sizes. E7.2 The §28 guard topologies are re-reported with their `A_eff` cost, and the joint frontier is published. E7.3 The roles whose `A_eff = 1` are named explicitly in §18. E7.4 No anonymity claim anywhere in the AXON specification survives without a scope and a number attached — audited by a documentation pass that is itself an exit criterion |
| **Residual risks** | The model is only as good as its prior. Real user behaviour is more distinguishable than any model assumes. A small network has small `A_eff` under every mechanism, and the early network's honest value is close to 1 |
| **New attacks introduced** | **Guard sharing concentrates**: larger shared guard sets raise `A_eff` and simultaneously raise the value of compromising one guard — the §34.1 trade in the other direction. **Popularity equalisation** for services costs bandwidth and may itself be a distinguisher. **The measurement tool is an attacker's tool**: it computes exactly what an adversary wants to know about a target population |

### 34.5 What this workstream does NOT establish

- Any actual anonymity. It builds the instrument that says how much there is.
- That the numbers will be acceptable. §34.1 suggests they will not be, at any
  plausible early network size.
- That the model captures real behaviour. Timing, usage patterns and application
  fingerprints dominate in practice and are largely outside the model.
- A single headline figure. There is no such thing as "AXON's anonymity set", and
  any future document that quotes one is misusing this work.

## 35. Workstream 8 — Bandwidth Measurement Without a Central Authority

### 35.1 The attack that defeats the current design

R14 specifies "bounded self-report plus delivery receipts plus bond". Delivery
receipts signed by adjacent relays are forgeable by **reciprocal inflation**:

```text
   A and B collude. A signs receipts attesting B delivered 1 Gbps.
   B signs receipts attesting A delivered 1 Gbps.
   Marginal cost: two signatures. No traffic is carried.
   Both gain selection weight proportional to a capacity neither has.
```

Any receipt scheme in which the attester benefits from the attestation, or is
indifferent to it, fails to this. The fix is structural, not cryptographic:
**attestation must come from a party with an incentive to report accurately.**

In AXON that party is the **client**. A client wants working circuits; it gains
nothing from inflating a relay's reported capacity and is actively harmed by
selecting a relay that cannot carry its traffic. Clients are also anonymous,
which is the complication: a client-signed receipt naming a circuit is a
deanonymisation vector, so receipts must be **blind-signed and aggregated**,
reusing the unlinkable-token machinery §14 already specifies for relay payment
(R11). The two mechanisms want the same primitive, which is a genuine
architectural economy.

### 35.2 The composite weight

No single signal is trustworthy; the design combines five, each bounding a
different lie:

```text
   claimed        self-reported capacity          bounds the OPTIMISTIC case
   observed       client-attested delivery        the only incentive-aligned signal
   receipts       blind-signed, aggregated        unlinkable, so clients can attest safely
   stake          bond-bounded claim ceiling      caps inflation by capital
   history        exponentially-weighted record   makes short-term lies expensive
   diversity      prefix/ASN caps                 caps concentration regardless of claim

   weight = min( claimed ,
                 ceiling(stake) ,
                 quantile_q(observed over window) ) · reliability(history)
```

The `min` is the point. A relay's weight is capped by the *most pessimistic*
credible signal, so inflating any one signal gains nothing; an adversary must
inflate all of them simultaneously, and `observed` requires either real capacity
or a population of colluding clients large enough to shift a quantile.

### 35.3 The seventeen fields

| Field | Content |
|---|---|
| **Threat model** | Colluding measurers; fabricated capacity; Sybil measurers; selective service (serve measurers well, everyone else badly); reciprocal inflation; bandwidth withholding; strategic throttling; and joint optimisation with §33's capital attack |
| **Current AXON weakness** | Receipts are attested by parties who benefit from inflation. No quantile logic, no reliability history, no measured `γ`. R14 names the gap and stops |
| **Security objective** | `γ ≤ 2` — an adversary cannot obtain more than twice its true capacity in selection weight — under collusion up to 20 % of clients, with `ε_bw` characterised |
| **Candidate mechanisms** | The §35.2 composite; probabilistic audits with unpredictable challenge timing; multi-observer aggregation with outlier rejection; stake-bounded ceilings; reliability decay; end-to-end throughput attestation by clients rather than hop-by-hop by relays |
| **Mechanisms rejected** | **Central bandwidth authority** — the thing being replaced; also a censorship and compromise point, and Tor's own operational history with bandwidth authorities shows it is not a solved problem even when centralised. **Pure self-report** — trivially gamed. **Relay-to-relay receipts as the primary signal** — defeated by §35.1. **Payment volume as a proxy for bandwidth** — an adversary paying itself inflates for free |
| **Protocol changes** | Client attestation messages; blind-signature issuance and redemption; audit challenge/response; descriptor carries claimed capacity and bond reference |
| **Cryptographic changes** | Blind signatures for unlinkable attestation — **shared with §14's token design and specified once, not twice**. Care required: the same token must not be usable to link an attestation to a payment |
| **DHT changes** | Aggregated measurement records as a record class, signed by aggregators and bonded; individual attestations never published |
| **Economic changes** | Bond-bounded claim ceiling; slashing for a relay whose observed delivery is persistently and materially below its claim; aggregator bonding on the §12.6 pattern |
| **Implementation changes** | `accounting/measure.go`, `accounting/attest.go`, aggregator role, `routing/select.go` integration |
| **Simulation methodology** | Adversary sweeps over colluding client fraction, colluding relay fraction, and selective-service strategies, measuring achieved `γ` — again with the adversary **optimising**, not following a fixed script |
| **Adversarial test methodology** | Reciprocal inflation pairs; a relay that serves audit challenges well and real traffic badly (the hardest case, since audits are distinguishable from traffic unless they are indistinguishable by construction); Sybil client populations manufacturing attestations |
| **Metrics** | `γ` under each collusion level; `ε_bw` distribution against ground truth in the test network; selection-weight error; cost per unit of inflation |
| **Milestones** | M8.1 ground-truth harness on the local network. M8.2 composite weight implemented. M8.3 blind attestation, jointly with §14. M8.4 collusion sweep. M8.5 comparison against a simulated central authority. M8.6 recommended parameters with `γ` stated |
| **Exit criteria** | E8.1 `ε_bw` measured against ground truth on a network where true capacity is known. E8.2 `γ ≤ 2` at 20 % colluding clients — **falsified by the sweep, and failure is a legitimate reported outcome**. E8.3 Reciprocal inflation between colluding relays yields no weight gain — falsified by any gain. E8.4 A selective-service relay is detected within a stated window. E8.5 **The comparison against a central authority is published even if the central baseline wins** — §27.2 forbids suppressing that result |
| **Residual risks** | Majority collusion defeats any peer-measurement scheme. Selective service is hard to detect when audits are distinguishable from real traffic. Clients attesting over circuits add latency and a new message class to fingerprint |
| **New attacks introduced** | **Attestation withholding** — clients that decline to attest starve honest relays of the signal, a slow denial attack. **Aggregator capture** — the aggregator sees the attestation stream; bonding makes it untrusted but not blind. **Blind-token linkage** — if §14's payment tokens and §35's attestation tokens share an issuance epoch, redemption patterns may correlate a payer with an attester, which would undo R11's unlinkability; this must be explicitly prevented and tested |

### 35.4 The comparison the prompt demands, stated honestly

| | Central authority (Tor-style) | AXON composite |
|---|---|---|
| Accuracy | Higher — a dedicated measurer with no stake in the outcome | Lower; bounded by quantile logic |
| Manipulation resistance | Good against relays, none against the authority itself | Bounded `γ` against relays; no authority to compromise |
| Failure mode | Authority compromise is total and silent | Degradation is gradual and partially detectable |
| Censorship | The authority can exclude any relay | No party can |
| Operational cost | A handful of well-run scanners | Every client contributes a little |
| Track record | Deployed for years, with known measurement problems | None |

**The honest expectation is that the central baseline measures more accurately.**
The decentralised design is not chosen because it measures better; it is chosen
because R14 refuses the authority, and the workstream's job is to quantify what
that refusal costs in `ε_bw` and `γ`. If the cost turns out to be extreme — if
`γ` cannot be held below 2 at any plausible parameters — that is a finding that
should propagate back to R14 rather than be absorbed quietly.

### 35.5 What this workstream does NOT establish

- Accuracy under majority collusion. Nothing achieves that.
- That the early network can measure anything useful. With few clients, quantiles
  over attestations are noise.
- That audits are indistinguishable from real traffic. If they are
  distinguishable, selective service defeats them, and making them
  indistinguishable is `[NEEDS RESEARCH]`.
- That the blind-token sharing with §14 is safe. It is an economy and a risk, and
  E8.5's companion test exists because sharing a primitive across two subsystems
  is exactly how unlinkability properties are lost.

## 36. The Unified Adversarial Simulator

### 36.1 One simulator is the wrong answer

The brief asks for a simulator spanning millions of nodes *and* packet-level
traffic analysis. Those are incompatible fidelities, and building one tool that
claims both produces a tool that is trusted for neither. The programme builds
**two engines with one configuration language, one adversary specification, and
one result format**, and is explicit about which questions each may answer.

```text
   ENGINE A — POPULATION            ENGINE B — PACKET
   ────────────────────             ─────────────────
   10³ – 10⁶ nodes                  10² – 10³ nodes
   event/epoch granularity          packet granularity, real cell codec
   Monte-Carlo + analytic           discrete-event, real timing
   answers: P_dea, P_ecl, T_det,    answers: classifier precision, overhead,
            C(x,y), γ, A_eff                 latency, correlation TPR/FPR
   CANNOT answer: anything about    CANNOT answer: anything about population
            packet timing                     scale or long horizons
```

A result from Engine A about traffic analysis, or from Engine B about network
scale, is inadmissible. §36.5's cross-validation is how the two are kept honest
where their domains overlap.

### 36.2 Shared substrate

| Component | Contents |
|---|---|
| **Topology model** | Node population with bandwidth distribution, ASN and prefix assignment, geographic placement, churn process. Distributions are either measured (and cited) or synthetic (and flagged in every result that uses them) |
| **Adversary specification** | Declarative: budget, strategy, `f` target, collusion structure, observation points, adaptivity. **Strategies must optimise**, not follow a script — a fixed naive adversary produces a flattering number and §33.3 and §35.3 both require the optimising form |
| **Configuration** | A single declarative file per experiment: topology, adversary, mechanism parameters, horizon, trial count, and a **seed**. Reproducibility is a hard requirement, not a nicety — a result that cannot be regenerated bit-for-bit from its config is not a result |
| **Result format** | JSONL, one record per trial or per cell, with the config hash embedded. Aggregation is a separate step so raw output can be re-analysed without re-running |
| **Sweep harness** | `f ∈ {0.01, 0.05, 0.10, 0.20, 0.30, 0.40, 0.50}` × `T ∈ {1 d, 1 w, 1 m, 3 m, 1 y}` as the default grid, with per-workstream extensions |

### 36.3 What each engine models

**Engine A** — path selection under the §33 weighting; guard topologies including
layered sets; tunnel-pool construction and rotation; DHT keyspace, `KadID`
rotation and lookup with `d` disjoint paths; churn; eclipse strategies; chain
availability as an on/off resource; storage placement and repair; the accounting
plane as a weight input. It does **not** model bytes.

**Engine B** — the real cell codec and framing from §8.1, real padding machines,
real QUIC stream behaviour where feasible, and trace capture at configurable
observation points. It reuses the §21 local multi-node environment rather than
reimplementing the protocol, which is the only way its results say anything about
the actual implementation.

### 36.4 The honesty requirements

1. **Synthetic distributions are labelled in the output**, not only in the
   documentation, so a plot cannot be lifted out of context.
2. **Every published result carries its config hash and seed.**
3. **Negative results are published in the same format as positive ones**, in the
   same repository, with equal prominence.
4. **The adversary model is versioned.** Improving the adversary invalidates
   earlier results, and the invalidation is recorded rather than the old numbers
   silently remaining.
5. **No result is reported without its uncertainty.** Monte-Carlo output gets
   confidence intervals; a point estimate from 100 trials is not a finding.

### 36.5 Cross-validation

Where the engines overlap — circuit lifetime effects, multiplexing, the observable
consequences of guard topology — both must produce compatible answers on a shared
scenario, and a discrepancy blocks publication until it is explained. Where an
analytic model exists (§28.1, §33.2, §34.1), it is checked against Engine A on
the same scenario, and the analytic form is preferred for reporting because it
generalises.

---

## 37. Quantitative Security Targets

Targets, with the rationale for each. **Where no defensible rationale exists the
row is marked `RESEARCH REQUIRED` and the establishing experiment is named** —
inventing a number would be worse than admitting there is not one.

| # | Metric | Target | Adversary | Measurement | Rationale |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| P1 | `P_dea(365 d)` for a service | < 0.05 | `f = 0.05` persistent, active forced sampling | Engine A, topology sweep | Chosen so that a service surviving a year at a 5 % adversary is the design point; the 5 % figure is itself `RESEARCH REQUIRED` — it is a plausible relay-population share for a funded adversary, not a measured one |
| P1 | `P_dea(365 d)` for a client | `RESEARCH REQUIRED` | — | Engine A curve published | §28.6: a universal client target is false precision. Experiment: characterise the curve and let deployments choose |
| P2 | Storage capacity fraction for global removal of one object | > `(n−k)/n` of holders, i.e. **> 3 of 8** at RS 6+3 | Coalition of storage operators | Analytic from the deployed coding parameters | Follows directly from erasure coding; it is the one abuse-related number that is exactly computable |
| P2 | Policy propagation latency | < 1 h to subscribed operators | — | Engine A, issuer-subscription graph | Matches DHT record propagation; no stronger claim is defensible |
| P2 | Issuer concentration (top-1 subscription share) | `RESEARCH REQUIRED` | Dominant-issuer adversary | Engine A over simulated time | No defensible threshold exists — the question is whether concentration occurs at all (E2.4) |
| P3 | `P_ecl` | < 0.01 | `f = 0.20` of selection opportunities | Engine A eclipse sweep | Two orders of magnitude below the adversary's share; chosen as falsifiable, and `RESEARCH REQUIRED` on whether it is achievable |
| P3 | `T_det` | ≤ 2 epochs (48 h) | `f ≤ 0.30` | Engine A | Two epochs allows one full SRV rotation before an alarm, avoiding churn false positives |
| P4 | `k_src` | ≥ 3 independent (operator, ASN, ideally implementation) | Provider censorship | Code audit + fault injection | Three is the minimum that survives one failure and one lie while leaving a majority; the independence definition matters more than the count |
| P4 | `S_max` | FULL: 19.2 min (finality). SNAPSHOT: declared per deployment, hard refusal at expiry | Stalling provider | §13.3 modes, fault injection | Finality is Ethereum's, not a choice. The snapshot bound is a deployment parameter and §12.6 already carries the machinery |
| P4 | Recovery after 1 week isolation | Verified head restored, no incorrect answer served during isolation | Total chain isolation | Fault injection | Correctness must never degrade; only freshness may |
| P5 | WF classifier precision at `p = 10⁻³` | `RESEARCH REQUIRED` — baseline must be measured first | Single-point observer with a retrained classifier | Engine B, open-world | Setting a target before the undefended baseline exists would be arbitrary. Experiment: M5.2 |
| P5 | Padding overhead | ≤ 50 % bandwidth, ≤ 100 ms added median latency | — | Engine B | The budget beyond which `INTERACTIVE` stops being interactive; a design constraint rather than a security target |
| P5 | Flow-correlation TPR at FPR = 10⁻³ | **No target.** Expected result: correlation succeeds | Two-ended observer | Engine B | §32.1: the honest expected outcome is IMPOSSIBLE, and a target would imply a defence that is not being claimed |
| P6 | `C(0.20, 30 epochs)` | Published as a formula in `S_h`, `r`, `c_infra`, with worked values | Optimising adversary across stake, identities, prefixes | Engine A optimiser | No absolute currency target is defensible when `S_h` is unknown; the deliverable is the function, not a number |
| P6 | Splitting gain under chosen `w`, `B_min` | ≤ 1.2× | Sybil-splitting adversary | Analytic + Engine A | §33.1 shows splitting gain is the failure mode of concave weighting; 1.2× is a pre-registered tolerance, `RESEARCH REQUIRED` on whether it is achievable at acceptable `B_min` |
| P7 | `A_eff`, `A_eff∞` per role | Measured and published; **no threshold** | Per adversary class | §34 tool | §34.5: a single headline figure would be a misuse of the work. The target is the instrument existing and being used |
| P8 | `γ` (inflation factor) | ≤ 2 | 20 % colluding clients, colluding relay pairs | Engine A + ground-truth harness | Beyond 2×, selection weight stops tracking capacity usefully; the threshold is engineering judgement and is marked as such |
| P8 | `ε_bw` vs ground truth | `RESEARCH REQUIRED` | — | Local network with known capacity | No prior exists for a composite decentralised estimator; M8.1 establishes it |

**Seven of nineteen rows are `RESEARCH REQUIRED`.** That is the accurate state of
the design, and §27.2 forbids replacing them with plausible-looking numbers.

## 38. Phases P17–P26

### 38.1 Ordering, and why it is not the brief's order

The brief's numbering implies intersection resistance first. **§26.3 requires the
anonymity model first**: P1, P5 and P7 share a posterior, and mechanisms cannot be
evaluated before the instrument that measures them exists. The programme
therefore reorders, keeping the brief's phase numbers so cross-references remain
usable:

```text
   P23 Anonymity measurement ──────────────┐  the instrument; everything
        │                                  │  downstream reports its numbers
        ├──────────────┬──────────────┐    │
        ▼              ▼              ▼    │
   P17 Intersection  P21 Traffic   P22 Economic ◄── sets f, the input to all
        │              analysis      calibration    of the above
        │              │              │
        │              │              ▼
        │              │         P24 Bandwidth measurement
        │              │              │  (P22 and P24 jointly determine
        │              │              │   selection weight, hence f)
        └──────────────┴──────────────┘
                       │
   P19 Eclipse ◄───────┼───────► P20 Chain access
    (mutually dependent: the chain anchors eclipse detection;
     eclipse of chain access is what P20 must prevent)
                       │
   P18 Abuse governance (independent of all of the above)
                       │
                       ▼
   P25 Unified simulation ──► P26 Integrated validation
```

### 38.2 The phases

Effort is engineer-months with a confidence rating. **Research phases have
unbounded tails**; the ranges below are for reaching a *reportable result*,
including a negative one, not for reaching success.

| Phase | Prerequisites | Deliverables | Effort | Conf. | Risk |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **P23** Anonymity measurement | §21 test env | Formal model; measurement tool; per-role baseline at three network sizes; audit of every anonymity claim in the specification | 3–6 em | **High** | Low — mathematics and tooling, no protocol change |
| **P22** Economic / Sybil calibration | P9b, `StakeVault` | §33.1 analysis reviewed; parameter search; adversary optimiser; `C(x,y)` surface; recommended `w`, `B_min`, `L`, caps | 6–12 em | Medium | Medium — the result may be that the price is low |
| **P24** Bandwidth measurement | P22, §14 blind tokens | Ground-truth harness; composite weight; blind attestation; collusion sweep; central-authority comparison | 10–20 em | **Low** | **High** — may not reach `γ ≤ 2`; shares a primitive with §14 |
| **P17** Intersection resistance | P23 | Analytic model; layered guards; forced-sampling limits; topology sweep with joint `P_dea`/`A_eff` frontier | 6–12 em | Medium | Medium — service side likely succeeds, client side likely does not |
| **P21** Traffic-analysis defence | P23, Engine B | Trace harness; baseline attacks; padding machines; defended evaluation; §32.3 dual-use experiment; correlation study | 12–24 em | **Low** | **High** — the field's results age badly and the correlation result is expected negative |
| **P19** Eclipse resistance | P20 (anchor), §7 | Eclipse simulator; view digests; SRV-seeded sampling; bootstrap diversity; chain anchor or its abandonment | 8–15 em | Medium | Medium — anchor design is unresolved (§30.2c) |
| **P20** Decentralized chain access | §12, light client | Multi-source with independence policy; DHT-carried evidence; relayer plurality; isolation recovery | 10–18 em | Medium | Medium — 2.7 GB/yr in the DHT is a real load |
| **P18** Abuse governance | §10, §12 | Taxonomy; five local mechanisms; assertion format and composition; removal-cost figure; concentration simulation; the §29.6 statement | 6–12 em | Medium | Medium — the honest outcome is partly a refusal to build |
| **P25** Unified simulation | P17–P24 | Engines A and B; shared config and adversary language; sweep harness; cross-validation | 12–20 em | Medium | Medium — scope creep is the main risk; the two-engine split is the mitigation |
| **P26** Integrated validation | P25 | Joint sweeps; interaction study; updated threat model; updated production criteria; the §40 answer | 6–12 em | Medium | Medium — interactions may undo individual results |

**Programme total: 79–151 engineer-months**, with the wide range driven almost
entirely by P21 and P24. A realistic reading is that this is a multi-year effort
for a small team, and that P23 and P22 — the two cheapest and highest-confidence
phases — should be done first regardless of whether the rest is funded, because
they produce the numbers that tell you whether the rest is worth funding.

### 38.3 Per-phase exit criteria and non-establishment

Each phase's falsifiable exit criteria are given in its workstream: E1.x §28.3,
E2.x §29.4, E3.x §30.3, E4.x §31.3, E5.x §32.4, E6.x §33.3, E7.x §34.4, E8.x
§35.3. P25's exit is §36.4's five honesty requirements being enforced by the
harness rather than by convention. P26's exit is §40 being written with every
row of §27.1 resolved to one of the four outcomes.

**What every phase does NOT establish, stated once because it applies to all of
them:** simulation results are not deployment results. Every number in this
programme is produced against modelled populations with assumed distributions,
and the relationship between those and a real network is itself unestablished.
§26.3's reduction, §33.1's concavity argument and §34.1's guard arithmetic are
analytic and will survive; everything measured in a simulator is provisional
until a real network exists to check it against.

### 38.4 Interactions that must be tested jointly

| Interaction | Why it matters |
|---|---|
| P22 ↔ P24 | Together they determine selection weight, hence `f`, hence every other result. An error here propagates everywhere |
| P17 ↔ P23 | Guards trade `P_dea` against `A_eff`; neither may be reported alone |
| P19 ↔ P20 | The chain anchors eclipse detection; eclipse can target chain access |
| P21 ↔ P23 | Padding changes the observation, hence the posterior, hence `A_eff` |
| P18 ↔ P12/P22 | Bonded complaints make abuse response a wealth test; the abuse design must not inherit the plutocracy of the economic design |
| P21 ↔ P22 | Padding costs bandwidth the accounting plane pays for; relays have an incentive to disable it |

## 40. Updated Threat Model, Readiness Criteria, and the Answer

### 40.1 Threat-model deltas

§18 is amended, not replaced. Each mitigation gets a row stating what it
addresses, what it does not, what it assumes, and what it introduces — the
existing four-column discipline extended:

| Mitigation | Addresses | Does **not** address | Assumes | Introduces |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Layered guards (§28) | Guard discovery against services | Client-side long-term exposure; availability leakage | `f` is correctly measured (§35) | Layer-targeting; L1 concentration |
| Policy assertions (§29) | Operator-local enforcement for nine abuse classes | Global removal; legal exposure | Operators choose issuers independently | Subscription inference; concentration |
| View digests + anchor (§30) | Eclipse detection | Eclipse recovery without any honest channel | Chain access survives (§31) | Digest poisoning; false-alarm steering |
| Multi-source chain access (§31) | Provider censorship, stalling, unavailability | Broadcast verification; Ethereum-level failure | ≥ 3 genuinely independent sources exist | Endpoint-discovery manipulation |
| Padding machines (§32) | Website fingerprinting, bounded | End-to-end correlation | Classifier evaluation is done on defended traces | Machine fingerprinting; class leakage |
| Calibrated bonds (§33) | Cheap mass Sybil creation | Wealthy adversaries; plutocracy | `S_h` is substantial | Bond centralisation; slashing abuse |
| Anonymity measurement (§34) | Unquantified claims | Any actual anonymity | Model priors approximate reality | An adversary's analysis tool |
| Composite bandwidth weight (§35) | Reciprocal inflation, capital inflation | Majority collusion; selective service | Clients attest honestly and are numerous | Withholding; aggregator observation; token linkage |

**The rule from §7 of the Constitution stands unchanged**: every anonymity claim
is quantified and scoped, and the words *perfect anonymity*, *untraceable*,
*impossible to block* and *unbreakable* do not appear.

### 40.2 Updated MVP definition

§24's ladder (M1–M6) tests function. This programme adds a rung that tests
*knowledge*, and it should gate any public deployment:

> **M7 — The instrumented network.** On the local test network at ≥ 500 simulated
> nodes: `A_eff` and `A_eff∞` are computed and published for all eight roles;
> `P_ecl` and `T_det` are measured at `f = 0.20`; a verified chain read completes
> with all but one source hostile; the WF baseline is measured with precision
> reported at `p = 10⁻³`; and `C(0.20, 30)` is published as a formula.
> **Pass condition: the numbers exist and are published — not that they are good.**
> M7 is a knowledge gate, not a security gate.

### 40.3 Updated production-readiness criteria

Added to §22's existing gates, and all four are falsifiable:

1. Every `[UNSOLVED]` in §25 resolves to DEPLOYED, BOUNDED, IMPOSSIBLE or REFUTED
   in §27.1's matrix, with evidence.
2. No anonymity claim in the user-facing documentation lacks a scope and a number.
3. The quantified residual risks are stated in the operator documentation, in
   plain language, where an operator will actually read them — specifically that
   `INTERACTIVE` traffic is vulnerable to end-to-end correlation, that `A_eff` is
   in the hundreds rather than the network size, and that storage and gateway
   operators carry legal exposure that encryption does not remove.
4. The negative results are published alongside the positive ones.

### 40.4 What remains fundamentally unsolved

After this entire programme, on the honest expectation recorded in §27.1:

| Problem | Expected residual state |
|---|---|
| **End-to-end flow correlation** | Not solved and not solvable at interactive latency. Bounded only by the adversary's coverage |
| **Anonymity in a small network** | `A_eff` is bounded by the user population. The early network provides very little anonymity to anyone, and no mechanism changes this |
| **Sybil resistance without capital** | Converted to a price, not removed. Plutocratic by construction (§33.1) |
| **Global abuse response** | Deliberately absent. §29.6 makes it a permanent architectural property |
| **Eclipse recovery in a total partition** | Requires a channel the adversary does not control; the design makes that conjunction expensive, not impossible |
| **Ethereum as a systemic dependency** | Bounded (§31.5), never removed, while ownership is on-chain |
| **Bandwidth measurement under majority collusion** | Not solvable by peer measurement |
| **Long-term intersection against an always-online service** | Slowed by orders of magnitude, never eliminated |
| **The user's own behaviour** | Dominates every protocol property and is outside the system entirely (§18.21) |

### 40.5 The answer to the question the brief asks

> *Can AXON move from a network that openly acknowledges eight major weaknesses
> to one where each has a demonstrated mitigation, a quantified residual risk, or
> a demonstrated reason it cannot be solved?*

**Yes for six, partly for one, and no for one — and the distribution is the
finding.**

- **Demonstrated mitigation is plausible for three**: eclipse detection (P3),
  decentralized chain access (P4), and the local-enforcement half of abuse
  handling (P2). These are engineering, and the engineering is tractable.
- **Quantified residual risk is the realistic outcome for four**: intersection
  resistance (P1), economic Sybil cost (P6), anonymity-set size (P7), and
  bandwidth measurement (P8). Each ends with a number rather than a defence, and
  in at least two cases — plutocratic Sybil pricing and small-network anonymity —
  the number will be unflattering.
- **Demonstrated impossibility is the expected outcome for one**: end-to-end
  correlation of interactive traffic (P5), which no deployed low-latency system
  prevents and which AXON should stop implying it might.
- **The partial case is global abuse response**, which is half engineering and
  half a permanent architectural refusal (§29.6).

The programme's real value is not that it makes AXON safe. It is that it replaces
eight unquantified weaknesses with eight measured ones, and a system whose
weaknesses are measured can be deployed deliberately — matched to threat models
it actually serves, and honestly declined for those it does not. **That is a
better outcome than a system that believes it solved them.**

### 40.6 What this section does NOT establish

- That the programme will be executed. It is 79–151 engineer-months and the
  expected outcome for several phases is a negative result.
- That the expected outcomes in §27.1 are correct. They are predictions recorded
  to prevent retrospective optimism, and they may be wrong in either direction —
  including optimistically.
- That resolving all eight makes AXON safe to use for a targeted individual
  facing a state adversary. It does not, and §4's refusals stand unchanged.
- That the numbers, once produced, will be acted on. §27.2's rule against moving
  goalposts is a discipline, not a mechanism, and nothing in the architecture
  enforces it.

# Part VI — Multipath Transport and Traffic Aggregation

**A substrate that distributes one logical connection across several independent
overlay paths — and an honest account of what that costs.**

---

## 41. The Finding That Shapes Part VI

**Multipath is two mechanisms with opposite privacy signs, and they must never be
evaluated together.**

```text
   Against a SINGLE-POINT observer          Against a MULTI-POINT observer
   (website fingerprinting, §32.1a)         (flow correlation, §32.1b)
   ────────────────────────────────         ──────────────────────────────
   Each observer sees only 1/N of the       The adversary now has N chances
   trace. Burst structure, volume and       to be on a path instead of one,
   timing are all fragmented.               and the N sub-flows share a
                                            global sequence structure that
   MULTIPATH HELPS — and it is one of       LINKS them to each other.
   the few defences that helps here
   without paying padding overhead.         MULTIPATH HURTS.
```

The second effect deserves emphasis because it is a *new* primitive rather than a
quantitative worsening: splitting one logical stream across N paths creates N
flows that an adversary can **confirm belong together** from their interleaved
global sequence numbers and their complementary gap structure. A single-path
design offers no such confirmation. An adversary sitting on two of four paths
learns not only that it holds two flows, but that those two flows are the same
user's — which is exactly the linkage the anonymity layer exists to prevent.

Two consequences bind the rest of Part VI:

1. **Performance aggregation and anonymity are separate optimisation objectives**
   and are given separate metrics, separate targets and separate modes (§49).
   The roadmap must never report a throughput gain as though it were free.
2. **The relay-exposure arithmetic changes.** With `N` paths of 3 hops and pinned
   guards shared across paths, the client's traffic passes through `1 + 2N`
   distinct relays instead of 3:

   | `N` | Distinct relays touched | `P(≥1 hostile relay)` at `f = 0.05` | at `f = 0.10` |
   |---|---|---|---|
   | 1 | 3 | 0.143 | 0.271 |
   | 2 | 5 | 0.226 | 0.410 |
   | 4 | 9 | 0.370 | 0.613 |
   | 8 | 17 | 0.582 | 0.833 |

   Each hostile relay sees only `1/N` of the stream, which is the §41 trade in
   numbers: **more observers, each with less.** Whether that is a net gain
   depends entirely on which adversary is being modelled, and §48 is where it is
   settled rather than asserted.

### 41.1 What is actually gained, and it is not linear bandwidth

The brief's framing — 50 + 30 + 20 Mbps ≈ 100 Mbps — is the outcome multipath
almost never delivers in an onion network. The binding constraints, in the order
they usually bind:

| Constraint | Why it binds | Does adding paths help? |
|---|---|---|
| **Client uplink** | All paths share it | **No.** If the client's own link is the bottleneck, aggregation gains exactly zero |
| **Exit / far-side capacity** | For clearnet, all paths converge (§42) | **No**, when one exit terminates the connection |
| **Reassembly buffer** | Buffer ≥ `RTT_max × Σ rᵢ` | No — it is a *cost* that grows with paths |
| **Slowest-path head-of-line blocking** | One stalled path blocks the receive window | No, and it can make throughput *worse* than single-path |
| **Per-relay share** | Volunteer relays are the scarce resource | Yes — this is the real source of gain |
| **Per-path latency** | Scheduler can pick the faster path per chunk | **Yes — and this is the most reliable gain of all** |

**The honest expectation: the dependable wins from multipath are latency,
resilience and tail-behaviour, not throughput multiplication.** Throughput gain
is real only when the per-relay share is the binding constraint and the client
uplink is not — which in a bandwidth-starved volunteer network is common enough
to be worth building for, but is not the default case and must be measured
(MP6, §50).

This is the same conclusion Tor's deployed traffic-splitting work reached: the
benefit is dominated by choosing the better path per chunk rather than by summing
capacity, and the design there deliberately keeps a *shared exit* for reasons
§42.3 develops.

### 41.2 The capacity-ethics problem, stated early

A client using `N` paths consumes `N` relays' scarce capacity for one user's
traffic. In a volunteer network this is a commons problem, and an aggressive
default turns AXON into a system where the users who configure the most paths
receive the most of a donated resource.

**Ruling (R20): path count is a policy the accounting plane may price, and the
default is conservative.** `N = 2` for interactive, `N ≤ 4` for bulk, higher only
where §14's accounting exists to charge for it. A performance mode that consumes
8 relay-paths per connection is a mode for a paying user or a well-provisioned
private deployment, not a default.

---

## 42. Architecture and Layer Placement

### 42.1 The new layer

Multipath goes **above the circuit layer and below the stream API** — a new L4.5
in §3's stack, and it is genuinely a separate layer rather than a feature of L4:

```text
  L8   INFRASTRUCTURE API        one logical connection, N is not visible
  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  L4.5 MULTIPATH TRANSPORT       split · schedule · reassemble · recover
         │   global sequence space, one logical session
         │
  L4   TUNNEL / CIRCUIT          N independent circuits, each 3+ hops
         │   per-circuit cells, per-hop AEAD, per-circuit keys (§8.3)
  L3   DHT · L2 PEER · L1 TRANSPORT · L0 INTERNET
```

The separation the brief asks for, stated as the rule §3's layer contract already
implies: **routing decides how traffic moves; the multipath substrate decides how
it is distributed.** L4.5 may ask L4 for a path with stated properties; it may
not choose relays, see IP addresses, or influence circuit construction beyond a
diversity request. L4 may report a path's observed capacity and liveness; it may
not see the logical stream.

### 42.2 Why not simply run multipath QUIC end-to-end

The obvious implementation — run Multipath QUIC between client and exit, over
circuits — is rejected, and the reason is worth stating because it will be
proposed again:

| Approach | Verdict | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| Multipath QUIC end-to-end over circuits | `REJECTED` | **Nested congestion control.** L1 links are already QUIC (§6.1). QUIC-over-QUIC gives two loss-recovery loops per hop, and the outer loop interprets inner-loop retransmission as congestion. This is a known pathology and the overhead compounds per hop |
| MPTCP | `REJECTED` | Needs kernel support and TCP options on the wire; incompatible with fixed 1024 B cells (§8.1); leaks a distinctive option fingerprint |
| Custom transport over the existing circuit abstraction | **`ADOPTED`** | Cells are already the unit; circuits already provide ordered, authenticated delivery per path; only sequencing, scheduling and reassembly need adding |
| Custom congestion control | `REJECTED` | §13's rule against inventing primitives extends here. The coupled-congestion-control literature from MPTCP (the LIA/OLIA/BALIA family) is adapted, not replaced — §45 |

So: **a purpose-built multipath layer over AXON circuits, reusing published
scheduling and coupled-congestion-control algorithms.** New code, no new
algorithms.

### 42.3 The topologies, and which are architecturally sound

This is the part of the brief that needs the sharpest answer, because two of the
three proposed topologies have a structural problem.

**(a) Overlay-internal: client ↔ anonymous service. `SOUND`.**

```text
            ┌─ G ─ M₁ ─ RP₁ ─┐
  Client ───┼─ G ─ M₂ ─ RP₂ ─┼─── Service        both ends are the endpoints
            └─ G ─ M₃ ─ RP₃ ─┘                    reassembly happens AT them
```

The service is the endpoint, so it reassembles. **No aggregator node exists, and
therefore no node sees the whole flow.** This is the clean case and it is the one
AXON should build first — it is also the case that matters most, since AXON's
purpose is anonymous services rather than clearnet exit.

**(b) Clearnet exit, single exit. `SOUND BUT LIMITED`.**

```text
            ┌─ G ─ M₁ ─┐
  Client ───┼─ G ─ M₂ ─┼─ Exit ─── Internet
            └─ G ─ M₃ ─┘
```

The exit terminates the TCP/QUIC connection to the destination, so it must
reassemble. It therefore sees the entire logical flow — which means **path
diversity buys nothing against the exit.** The N paths defend against middle
relays and against network observers on individual paths, and against nothing
else. This is the deployed-Tor shape and it is honest as long as its limit is
stated: multipath here is a defence against *middles and observers*, never
against the exit.

**(c) Clearnet exit, multiple exits with a separate aggregator. `REJECTED`.**

```text
            ┌─ … ─ Exit A ─┐
  Client ───┼─ … ─ Exit B ─┼─ Aggregator ─── Internet     ← the super-node
            └─ … ─ Exit C ─┘
```

The aggregator sees the full logical flow *and* the identity of every exit. It is
precisely the "centralised super-node that sees all traffic" the brief warns
against, and it is strictly worse than (b): (b)'s exit sees the flow, and (c)'s
aggregator sees the flow *plus* the path structure, while adding a node whose
compromise is catastrophic and whose operation is a standing correlation point.
**A separate aggregator node is not adopted in any mode.**

The general rule, which is the answer to the brief's §10 question:
**aggregation must happen at an endpoint, never at an intermediary.** Where both
ends are inside the overlay, that is free. Where one end is the clearnet, the
exit is the endpoint and the limit in (b) applies.

### 42.4 Decision table

| Decision | Problem it solves | Derived from | What we changed | Alternatives rejected | New vulnerability |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Multipath at L4.5, above circuits | Aggregation without coupling to routing | Tor's circuit-splitting work; MPTCP's layering | Operates on cells over circuits rather than packets over IP | Multipath QUIC end-to-end (nested CC); MPTCP (kernel, fingerprint) | A new layer with its own state, its own bugs, and its own fingerprint |
| Endpoint-only aggregation | Avoids a super-node | Tor's shared-exit approach | Stated as a general rule and applied to the overlay-internal case, which Tor has no analogue for | Separate aggregator node (§42.3c) | For clearnet, the exit still sees everything |
| Shared guard set across paths | Stops entry exposure multiplying by N | §28's layered guards | Guards pinned per isolation context, not per path | Independent guards per path (multiplies §28.1's exposure by N) | Concentrates all paths' entry at one or two relays — a shared failure and correlation point |
| Conservative default `N` (R20) | Volunteer capacity is a commons | None — this is an AXON-specific consequence of §14 | Path count becomes an accounted resource | Unbounded client-chosen N | Users perceive the default as slow and raise it, defeating the policy |

---

## 43. The Multipath Transport Substrate

### 43.1 Object model

```text
  LogicalSession        one per (client, destination) — survives path churn
     ├── session key material, independent of any path (§47)
     ├── global sequence space
     ├── reassembly buffer + receive window
     ├── retransmission state
     └── PathSet
```
